title: Citation-Consistent Voting for Permutation-Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
Paper [10] explicitly addresses the same problem of position bias in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems, stating: "LLM answers vary substantially across permutations of the retrieved set... This reveals a previously underexplored sensitivity to retrieval order." This matches the contribution's purpose of making RAG systems robust to retrieved-document ordering without training. Paper [17] also discusses positional bias in RAG systems, noting: "the positioning of retrieved passages within the input can degrade output quality." Both papers share the same objective at the problem-class level.

### Mechanism
No prior paper describes a mechanism substantively equivalent to Citation-Consistent Voting (CCV). While papers [3], [5], [8], [11], [13], and [25] discuss self-consistency or voting-based methods, they focus on selecting answers based on frequency, confidence, or token overlap, rather than aggregating citation-consistency scores across permutation-invariant document IDs. Paper [26] introduces citation-aware reasoning but does not involve permutation-invariant aggregation or document-ID mapping. None of these mechanisms match the technical primitive of CCV.

### Evaluation
Paper [10] evaluates position bias in RAG systems using a permutation-based setup, stating: "under a Top-5 retrieval setting... answers vary substantially across permutations." This matches the evaluation design of testing robustness to document order permutations. Paper [17] also evaluates positional bias in RAG systems, noting: "Standard RAG systems typically rely on a fixed top k retrieval strategy... Additionally, the positioning of retrieved passages within the input can degrade output quality." Both papers use permutation-based evaluation designs, covering the contribution's evaluation facet.

### Domain
Multiple prior papers, including [9], [10], [17], and [23], work in the general application area of retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for open-domain question answering. For example, paper [9] states: "RAG has emerged as a promising solution... particularly for knowledge-intensive tasks," and paper [10] focuses on "retrieval-permutation-induced hallucinations in RAG systems." The contribution operates within this established domain.
